title: The Cobbler Turned Doctor
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A very unskilful Cobbler, finding himself unable to make a living at his trade, gave up mending boots and took to doctoring instead. He gave out that he had the secret of a universal antidote against all poisons, and acquired no small reputation, thanks to his talent for puffing himself.

One day, however, he fell very ill; and the King of the country bethought him that he would test the value of his remedy. Calling, therefore, for a cup, he poured out a dose of the antidote, and, under pretence of mixing poison with it, added a little water, and commanded him to drink it.

Terrified by the fear of being poisoned, the Cobbler confessed that he knew nothing about medicine, and that his antidote was worthless. Then the King summoned his subjects and addressed them as follows: "What folly could be greater than yours? Here is this Cobbler to whom no one will send his boots to be mended, and yet you have not hesitated to entrust him with your lives!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Cobbler give up mending boots?
options: He is injured and can no longer work with his hands
He decides doctoring pays much better regardless of skill
He finds himself unable to make a living at his trade
He is ordered by the King to change professions

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Cobbler claim to have?
options: The secret of a universal antidote against all poisons
A rare cure passed down from his family
A license granted by the royal court
A collection of ancient medical texts

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Cobbler gain his reputation?
options: Thanks to curing several sick villagers
Thanks to a recommendation from a real doctor
Thanks to inheriting his father's practice
Thanks to his talent for puffing himself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the King do to test the Cobbler's remedy?
options: He asks another doctor to examine the antidote first
He mixes water into the antidote under the pretence of adding poison
He orders the Cobbler to drink real poison directly
He has the antidote tested on an animal first

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Cobbler confess when he is afraid of being poisoned?
options: That he had stolen the antidote recipe from a real doctor
That the King had misunderstood his true intentions
That he knew nothing about medicine and his antidote was worthless
That he had already cured himself once before

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the King say about the people entrusting their lives to the Cobbler?
options: That no one sent him boots to mend, yet they trusted him with their lives
That the Cobbler had earned their trust through years of service
That the people should have tested him earlier themselves
That the Cobbler deserved a second chance despite his failure

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the King's trick with the water succeed in exposing the Cobbler?
options: The water itself was somehow toxic to the Cobbler
The King secretly told the Cobbler what was in the cup beforehand
The antidote changed color when mixed with water
The Cobbler's fear reveals that he does not actually trust his own remedy

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what point is the King making by comparing the Cobbler's bootmaking reputation to his medical reputation?
options: The Cobbler was actually skilled at both trades equally
People trusted him with something far more important than what they never trusted him with in the first place
The King wanted to give the Cobbler a chance to prove himself as a bootmaker again
The people had always trusted the Cobbler with both boots and medicine

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "puffing himself" mean in "his talent for puffing himself"?
options: Working extremely hard without rest
Studying medicine in secret
Exaggerating his own abilities to impress others
Avoiding attention from the public

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A confident claim is not the same as real skill, and a clever test can expose the difference
Cobblers should never be allowed to change professions
Kings are always wiser than the common people they rule
Medicine is a profession too dangerous for self-taught practitioners

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Cobbler one day?
options: He is arrested for fraud
He loses all his money
He is challenged by a rival doctor
He falls very ill

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the King call for in order to test the remedy?
options: A written contract
A cup
A group of witnesses
A second doctor's opinion

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whom does the King address after the Cobbler's confession?
options: His personal guards
The Cobbler's family
His subjects
The other doctors in the kingdom

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the King choose to test the Cobbler personally rather than simply trusting the popular opinion of him?
options: He wants concrete proof rather than relying on a reputation built on self-promotion
He is personally afraid of being poisoned by someone else
He has never met the Cobbler in person before
He wants to publicly reward the Cobbler for his fame

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "no small reputation" suggest about how widely the Cobbler was believed?
options: Only a few people in the kingdom had ever heard of him
His reputation was mostly negative among the townspeople
His reputation was limited only to the royal court
A large number of people had come to trust his false claims

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "folly" mean in "What folly could be greater than yours"?
options: Bravery or courage
Foolishness or poor judgment
Wealth or prosperity
Curiosity or wonder

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Cobbler becomes a genuinely skilled doctor over time
A King punishes a Cobbler for practicing medicine without permission
A failed Cobbler poses as a doctor until the King's clever test exposes his fraud
A Cobbler cures the King of a real illness
